Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-4,-1),$ and passes through the point $(0,-3).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-4,-1),$ and so we have

$$
x+4=2pt,\,y+1=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(0,-3),$ we can substitute $x=0$ and $y=-3$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}4=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ -2 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+4=2(-2)t,\,y+1=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+4=-4t,\,y+1=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(3,3),$ and so we have

$$
x-3=2pt,\,y-3=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(7,5),$ we can substitute $x=7$ and $y=5$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}4=2pt \\ 2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$

$$

x-3=4t,\,y-3=2{t}^{2}.

questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y+1)^{2}=-(x-3)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(3,-1).$ So we have

$$
x-3=p{t}^{2},\,y+1=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-(x-3) \\ 4p(x-3) & =-(x-3) \\ 4p & =-1 \\ p & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-3=(-\frac{1}{4}){t}^{2},\,y+1=2(-\frac{1}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-3=-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2},\,y+1=-\frac{1}{2}t.
$$

Consider the following parametric equation of the parabola

$$
x-4=-\frac{2}{5}\,t,\,y+1=-\frac{4}{25}\,{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this parabola is

$(x\,-$
{{field-1}}$)^{2}=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =-\frac{5}{2}(x-4),\,{t}^{2}=-\frac{25}{4}(y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{5}{2}(x-4))}^{2} \\  & =\frac{25}{4}\,(x-4)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-\frac{25}{4}(y+1)$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{25}{4}\,(x-4)^{2} & =-\frac{25}{4}(y+1) \\ {(x-4)}^{2} & =-(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x+2=-\frac{1}{2}t,\,y+3=-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =-2(x+2),\,{t}^{2}=-4(y+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-2(x+2))}^{2} \\  & =4{(x+2)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-4(y+3)$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+2)}^{2} & =-4(y+3) \\ (x+2)^{2} & =-(y+3).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x+5=-2t,\,y+2=-{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =-\frac{x+5}{2},\,{t}^{2}=-(y+2).\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{x+5}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-(y+2)$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+5)^{2}}{4} & =-(y+2) \\ (x+5)^{2} & =-4(y+2).\end{aligned}
$$

What set of parametric equations, defined for $t\in(-\infty, \infty),$ generates the parabola shown below?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14007650/assets/1a75a5242f3636efac8def7fc62458e1c1c6972ca79a1ab6fd73af47be622a7a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-4,5),$ and passes through the point $(-2,3).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x - h = 2pt, \qquad y - k = pt^2,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k) = (-4,5),$ and so we have

$$
x + 4 = 2pt, \qquad y - 5 = pt^2.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-2, 3),$ we can substitute $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x + 4 = 2\left(-\dfrac12\right)t, \qquad y - 5 = \left(-\dfrac12\right)t^2 ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x + 4 = -t, \qquad y - 5 = -\dfrac12t^2 .
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(-3,2),$ and passes through the point $(1,0).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x - h = pt^2, \qquad y - k = 2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k) = (-3,2),$ and so we have

$$
x+3 = pt^2, \qquad y-2 = 2pt.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(1,0),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=0$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}4=p{t}^{2} \\ -2=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(-\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t^2, \qquad y -2 = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+3 = \dfrac{1}{4}t^2, \qquad y -2= \dfrac{1}{2}t .
$$

$$

$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =-\frac{x-1}{2},\,t=-\frac{y+1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{y+1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$
